newsitem.title: UK: Britain says N.Ireland decision "sad for all".
newsitem.headline: Britain says N.Ireland decision "sad for all".

text.p: Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said on Sunday that a decision to allow an Orange Order parade along the Catholic Garvaghy Road of Portadown was "a sad day for all of us".

"Many people will be angry with what has occurred and I ask for restraint," Mowlam told Belfast reporters, after residents of the area clashed overnight with police who seized control of the road to clear it for the Orange march.
"The decision which the chief constable (Ronnie Flanagan) had to take was in the interests of public safety for the whole of Northern Ireland and I support him," she said.
"When there is intransigence on both sides, two intransigent groups, neither of which would move, a decision had to be made for them," she said in her first public statement for 24 hours.
Mowlam said efforts to reach a compromise between the pro-British Orange Order and Catholic Irish nationalists had continued until the early hours of Sunday but failed.
"It (the decision) has been dictated by circumstances. I would have preferred it otherwise," she said.

She was speaking as the Orange Order began a march from the centre of Portadown to a prayer service at Drumcree Church before returning to the southern town along the Garvaghy Road, whose Catholic residents wanted the march stopped.
About a dozen people in Portadown were treated for injuries sustained when one of the biggest security operations mounted in Northern Ireland in recent years took control of Garvaghy Road.
Several were treated for wounds caused by police rubber bulleets fired to disperse the crowd, residents said.
Witnesses said tension was running high along the road after hundreds of police backed by British troops cordoned off the area and pushed back residents who tried to stop their advance.
The security forces lined the Garvaghy Road behind columns of armoured jeeps to prevent demonstrators trying to disrupt the parade due to pass later on Sunday.
The decision infuriated Portadown Catholics and there were indications that it had ignited Irish nationalist anger elsewhere in the province, police said.
They said a handful of cars had been hijacked and set alight in Catholic West Belfast, a stronghold of Irish nationalists.
Last year police banned the Orange Order from the Garvaghy Road section of the march but changed the decision after four days of Protestant rioting brought the province to its knees.
